newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmaker says China must cut pollution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmaker says China must cut pollution.

text.p: China must be required to limit its industrial pollution under an international treaty on global warming in order to get congressional support for the deal, the chairman of the House International Relations Committee said on Thursday.

"Treaties that impose heavier burdens on Americans than on other countries have been given a very rough ride in any Congress -- Republican or Democrat. Hopefully this draft treaty can be adjusted to ensure strong congressional support," New York Republican Benjamin Gilman said at a committee hearing.
The climate change treaty would be subject to Senate ratification, and Congress would need to approve the new laws needed to implement the treaty.
Gilman has signed on to a resolution that generally backs the Clinton administration's stance in talks to reduce pollution from fossil fuels that is heating the atmosphere.
But he said he wanted the resolution to specify that all countries, "and especially China," face the same timetables to limit their emissions.
China, with 1.2 billion people, is expected to pass the United States in carbon emissions in about 25 years. Per capita, the United States remains by far the biggest source of industrial emissions.

Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth said the administration was pursuing a middle ground that would gradually draw China and other developing countries into the treaty. However, it would not hold them to immediate obligations faced by industrialised countries that caused almost all of the existing pollution.
"We think we have the concept about right. No one should be exempt. We emit the most, so we have to act first, but others have to phase in over time," Wirth said.
The U.S. position is to call on developing countries that have significant emissions to agree to negotiate binding pollution limits that they would adopt by 2005.

Industrialised countries would adopt binding commitments in December that would result in significant reductions in emissions by 2010 under the U.S. position. However, the White House has not set targets and timetables for those reductions.

Gilman said the administration postion "could cut U.S. Gross Domestic Product by up to 3 percent and put our country at a serious competitive disadvantage in relation to China, South Korea and 120 other countries not covered by legally binding timetables."

A Senate resolution signed by 60 senators also calls for the United States to demand that developing countries face binding commitments to limit pollution in the same time limits as industrialised countries.
